performers: Hans Duhan, baritone; Ferdinand Foll, piano
question: How does repeating a song’s pattern change what it means?
intro: A dream of May flowers is cut off by a cockcrow and a cold, dark room, and then the whole pattern runs again. Three tempos alternate: a swaying dream, a fast waking and a slow, halting question.

sections.label: Introduction · three bars for the piano

cues.title: A dream in swaying 6/8
cues.text: The score is marked Etwas bewegt, somewhat moving, in 6/8. After a pickup and three bars for the piano, arpeggiated chords under a melody, the voice enters at about 0:16 over the same swaying figure.
cues.evidence: The marking, the 6/8 metre, a one-eighth pickup and the voice entry in bar 4 are in the OpenScore transcription (CC0); a boundary falls at 0:16 (novelty 0.39), and the opening window is −27.8 dB. The entry is proportioned from the score’s bars.

cues.title: Dream and waking
cues.text: In the first verse he dreams of bright flowers, as they bloom in May, of green meadows and merry birdsong. At the cockcrow his eyes open: it is cold and dark, and ravens screech from the roof.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, Frühlingstraum (Müller’s no. 21, Schubert’s song no. 11), first two stanzas (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. They are sung in bars 4–26 of the score (OpenScore), about 0:16–1:30 by proportion.

cues.title: The cockcrow: Schnell
cues.text: At about 1:00 the swaying stops and the tempo changes to Schnell, fast. The piano plays short, dry chords, each followed by rests, in place of the flowing figure.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 0:56 (novelty 0.49) and 1:04 (0.45); the level falls to −22.9 dB at 1:00 (1.0 attacks per second) before rising to −12.2 dB at 1:10. The score marks Schnell in bar 14 and sets eighth-note chords each followed by rests, for example, in bar 15, chord, two eighth rests, chord, two eighth rests (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

cues.title: Slow and halting
cues.text: At about 1:30 the tempo slows to Langsam, slow, and the metre changes to 2/4. Repeated chords that keep an A sounding in both hands set a halting rhythm.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 1:30 (novelty 0.47) and 1:34 (0.37); one of the loudest windows is 1:45. The score marks Langsam and 2/4 at bar 27, with repeated A’s in both hands (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

cues.title: Frost on the window
cues.text: In the third verse he asks who painted the leaves on the window panes. Then he turns on his listeners: will you laugh at the dreamer who saw flowers in winter?
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, Frühlingstraum (Müller’s no. 21, Schubert’s song no. 11), third stanza (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. It is sung in bars 28–42 of the score (OpenScore), about 1:32–1:56 by proportion.

cues.title: As above
cues.text: Near 2:00 the sound almost stops. From about 2:02 the first dream’s music returns, marked Wie oben, as above, and the voice joins fifteen seconds later. Its climax near 2:45, at −9.7 dB one of the song’s two loudest windows, is hotter than the first dream’s.
cues.evidence: The level is −26.9 dB at 2:00 with 0.0 attacks per second; boundaries at 1:56 (novelty 0.75) and 2:06 (0.38). A recurrence analysis matches 2.5–30.0 s with 123.5–151.0 s (offset 121 s, no transposition, similarity 0.94), so the second dream begins about 2:01. The score marks Wie oben and 6/8 at bar 44 and the voice returns at bar 48 (OpenScore). The loudest windows are 2:45 (−9.7 dB, 3.6 attacks per second) and 3:50 (−9.7 dB), then 1:45, 2:55 and 0:35; a boundary falls at 2:46 (0.47); the first dream’s loudest window is 0:35 (−11.3 dB).

cues.title: A second dream, a second waking
cues.text: In the fourth verse he dreams of love for love, of a beautiful girl, of hearts and kisses, of joy and bliss. When the cocks crow again, his heart wakes, and now he sits alone, thinking back over the dream.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, Frühlingstraum (Müller’s no. 21, Schubert’s song no. 11), fourth and fifth stanzas (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. They are sung in bars 48–70 of the score (OpenScore), about 2:17–3:36 by proportion and the recurrence offset.

cues.title: A group of twelve ends here
cues.text: Schubert composed the first twelve songs of Winterreise in February 1827. This was the eleventh, and with “Irrlicht”, “Rast” and “Einsamkeit” it closed his first group. Hans Gál counted it among the few brighter episodes of the cycle, whose placing he found wise.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Winterreise article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winterreise): composition in two parts of twelve and the first group’s closing songs. Hans Gál’s remark on Der Lindenbaum, Frühlingstraum and Die Post is cited in German Wikipedia, Am Brunnen vor dem Tore (https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Am_Brunnen_vor_dem_Tore).

cues.title: The cockcrow again
cues.text: After a quiet moment near 3:00 the Schnell returns at about 3:10, with the same short, dry chords as in the first waking.
cues.evidence: The level is −26.7 dB at 3:00 (0.6 attacks per second); boundaries at 3:00 (0.46), 3:10 (0.49) and 3:16 (0.39). The score marks Schnell at bar 58 and sets the text of waking and sitting alone in bars 58–70 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

cues.title: The question asked twice
cues.text: From about 3:36 the Langsam returns, with the halting chords of 1:30. The last question is sung twice, and one of the two loudest windows of the song, at 3:50, lies in it.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 81.5–110.0 s with 208.0–236.5 s (offset 126.5 s, no transposition, similarity 0.93), which places the second Langsam about 126 s after the first; boundaries at 3:44 (novelty 0.38), 3:48, 3:52 and 3:56 (0.47); the loudest 5-second windows are 2:45 and 3:50 (both −9.7 dB; 3.8 attacks per second at 3:50). In the score the final question “wann halt’ ich mein Liebchen im Arm?” is sung in bars 83–86 and the song ends in 2/4 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

cues.title: The last question
cues.text: He shuts his eyes again, and his heart still beats warm. When will the leaves at the window turn green? When will he hold his beloved in his arms?
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, Frühlingstraum (Müller’s no. 21, Schubert’s song no. 11), sixth stanza (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. It is sung in bars 72–86 of the score (OpenScore), from about 3:37 by the recurrence offset.

transitions.title: Three bars of piano, then the voice
transitions.from: Introduction · three bars for the piano
transitions.how: After a one-eighth pickup, three bars for the piano alone, in 6/8 and the score’s A major, set a swaying pulse with arpeggiated chords in the left hand under a right-hand melody. The voice enters in bar 4 without a change of tempo, as if the dream were the piano’s own music continued.
transitions.evidence: A boundary at 0:16 (novelty 0.39) and a rise in level from −27.8 dB at 0:00 to −20.6 dB at 0:10. The score has a pickup, piano alone in bars 1–3 and the voice from bar 4 (OpenScore); the recording is pitched lower than the score, so no key is claimed for it.

transitions.title: The dream stops
transitions.how: The swaying music stops. The word “Und” leads directly to Schnell, the score’s next tempo, and the piano switches to short, dry chords, each followed by rests. The cockcrow wakes him, and the accompaniment shrinks from a flowing figure to flat, pointed strokes. The flowing figure of the dream does not return until the second dream.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 0:56 (novelty 0.49) and 1:04 (0.45); the level is −22.9 dB at 1:00 and −12.2 dB at 1:10. The score marks Schnell in bar 14 and sets short chords with rests in bars 14–26 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

transitions.title: Faster, then slower
transitions.how: The fast cockcrow ends and the score drops to Langsam, now in 2/4 instead of 6/8. The repeated chords, which keep an A sounding in both hands, move more slowly and the rhythm halts as he looks at the frost patterns on the window. The change of tempo and metre together turns the music from action to reflection.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 1:30 (novelty 0.47) and 1:34 (0.37). The score marks Langsam and 2/4 at bar 27 and repeated chords that keep A sounding in bars 27–30 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

transitions.title: A pause, then the dream again
transitions.how: The Langsam question ends, and a near-silent window follows. Then the score returns to 6/8 with the marking Wie oben, as above: the swaying music of the first dream comes back, now for the words about love, and the piano plays four bars alone before the voice enters.
transitions.evidence: The level is −26.9 dB at 2:00 with 0.0 attacks per second; boundaries at 1:56 (novelty 0.75) and 2:06 (0.38); a recurrence analysis matches 2.5–30.0 s with 123.5–151.0 s (offset 121 s). The score marks 6/8 and Wie oben at bar 44, piano alone to bar 47 and the voice from bar 48 (OpenScore).

transitions.title: The second waking
transitions.how: The second dream rises to its loudest window near 2:45, then falls to a quiet window at 3:00. The score marks Schnell again in bar 58 and the short chords return, as in the first waking. The same device, a break in tempo and texture, now ends a longer dream. The text moves from the eyes to the heart.
transitions.evidence: Loudest windows 2:45 (−9.7 dB) and 2:55 (−10.8 dB), then −26.7 dB at 3:00; boundaries at 3:00 (0.46) and 3:10 (0.49). The score marks Schnell at bar 58 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

transitions.title: Slow again: the final question
transitions.how: The second cockcrow gives way to Langsam in 2/4, with the same repeated chords as at 1:30. The voice now asks when the leaves will turn green and when he will hold his beloved, and it asks twice. The song ends in the score on an A minor chord, with C naturals in both hands, straight after the question.
transitions.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches the first Langsam (81.5–110.0 s) with 208.0–236.5 s; boundaries at 3:44 (novelty 0.38), 3:48, 3:52 and 3:56 (0.47); the loudest windows are 2:45 and 3:50 (−9.7 dB). The score marks Langsam and 2/4 at bar 71 and the last question in bars 83–86, ending on an A minor chord in bar 88, A–C–E with C naturals in both hands (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

source.title: Schubert, Winterreise No. 11, Frühlingstraum, OpenScore Lieder transcription (CC0)
source.locator: pickup and bars 1–88; the voice is silent in bars 0–3, 27, 43–47, 71 and 87–88; times proportioned to the boundaries at 0:16, 1:04, 1:30 and 3:10 and the recurrence offsets of about 121–126 s between the two sequences, with the second dream’s voice entry (bar 48) about fifteen seconds after its start at about 2:02.

timeline.note: After the pause, four bars for the piano alone.
The last chords for the piano alone.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy names Kammersänger Hans Duhan, baritone of the Vienna State Opera, with Prof. Ferdinand Foll at the piano; the Internet Archive description names the same two performers. Utz reports that Duhan recorded nineteen songs with Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928 and the remaining five (Nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, 23) with Lene Orthmann on 11 July 1928, so Orthmann does not play on this side. The Commons file description names only Duhan.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: Utz measures this song at 4:11, the longest side of the set; no source consulted states the performing text or the key of the transfer. The transposition from the first edition and the absolute pitch of the transfer are not established here.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Internet Archive description of the disc that carries this side gives the recording date. Utz lists the same three Foll session days (27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928) without assigning songs to days, so the song-by-day assignment rests on the Internet Archive uploader’s labelling. Commons gives only the year 1928.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No source consulted names the studio or city of the session.

fields.value: Gramola Record (The Gramophone Company (Czechoslovakia) Limited), as printed on the scanned copy
fields.note: The label photograph of this scanned copy shows a Gramola Record imprint, whereas the photographed first disc carries the His Master’s Voice imprint; the photographed copies of this set carry both imprints. The label gives no date, and nothing here dates the first issue or shows that the audio transfer derives from the photographed copy.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy prints Cat. No. ES 386, and the Commons file name and the Internet Archive description agree.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: CK 2956, take 1 (run-out “Ck 2956” with I); side No. 11 (label number 0942032); reverse side: Einsamkeit (matrix BK 2957-2). Disc 6 of 12 of the set; 30 cm.
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy shows the matrix and take in the run-out; the Internet Archive description and the Commons file name give the same matrix and take. The set was issued as twelve discs, one song to a side (Utz). The photograph is of one copy and does not identify the copy from which the audio was transferred.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer engineer is named. The Commons file was uploaded on 11 August 2015 by the user Patachonf and re-uploaded on 10 and 15 February 2022 by the user Mitar; the Internet Archive item was added on 25 April 2019 by the uploader recordplayer78. These are upload facts, not transfer credits.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. Upload dates are not treated as transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Both hosts hold a FLAC file. The Commons duration (259.24 s) and the Internet Archive FLAC length (259.12 s) agree within 0.15 s, which suggests the same digitisation; which host received it first is not established, and the source disc, stylus, equalisation and noise treatment are undocumented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Both the music and the poem are out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828 and the poet Wilhelm Müller in 1827. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to this recording, attributed to 1928. The Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s assertion and is not treated as authority to waive any rights. The publication date of the original disc is not documented; the EU basis here depends on the recording being first published before 1963, which is inferred from its 1928 session. Not established as public domain in the United States.

composer.epithet: A Viennese songwriter who made the piano an equal narrator, and carried the harmonic dislocations of the Lied into symphonies and chamber music.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition with Antonio Salieri, 1812–16
Assistant in his father’s school; music tutor to the Esterházy family at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; thereafter chiefly an independent composer
Johann Michael Vogl · Josef von Spaun · Franz von Schober · Johann Mayrhofer · Moritz von Schwind
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and music for the stage
composer.background:
Schubert grew up in a schoolmaster’s household in Himmelpfortgrund, then a suburb of Vienna. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz taught him piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer supplied further instruction. Family quartet sessions put Franz on viola, between the melody and the bass: he knew chamber music from an inner part. In 1808 he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school. Its orchestra introduced him to Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven as a player, while Antonio Salieri began giving him composition lessons in 1812.

After leaving the school in 1813, he trained as a teacher and became an assistant in his father’s classroom. Composition continued around the timetable. Gretchen am Spinnrade, dated 19 October 1814, gives Goethe’s girl a right-hand spinning wheel, a left-hand treadle and a vocal line that repeatedly tries to escape them. Schubert was seventeen. In 1815 he wrote roughly 140 songs, including Erlkönig, as well as symphonies, church music and stage works. Voice and piano already carried distinct dramatic responsibilities in his songs.
